meta.title: Transformers & Attention: why Q·Kᵀ > recurrence
meta.subtitle: how a Transformer reads, weighs and predicts — from tokens to the next word

cover.summary: Self-attention lets every token look at every other token in one step, so Transformers train in parallel and capture long-range context far better than RNNs. These notes follow the data: tokens, embeddings, Q/K/V attention, heads, the block, training and the model families built on it.
cover.big_idea: every token looks at every other token — in parallel!
toc: 2. the big picture, tokens in → word out

sections.title: the big picture
sections.subtitle: tokens in, next word out

blocks.text: Before 2017 most sequence models were **RNNs** that read a sentence one word at a time, carrying a hidden state forward. That made training slow (no parallelism) and long-range memory weak. The Transformer from “Attention Is All You Need” (Vaswani et al., 2017) drops recurrence entirely and uses attention instead.

items: Input text is cut into tokens and each token becomes a vector (an embedding).
Positional information is added, because attention alone has no sense of word order.
A stack of identical blocks mixes information between tokens (attention) and then refines each token (feed-forward network).
A final linear layer + softmax turns the last vector into a probability for every word in the vocabulary.

blocks.text: Teacher's one-line summary: “attention is a soft dictionary lookup — each token asks a question, every token offers a key and a value.”
Test of escaping: a model name like <GPT-4> & friends, 5 > 3, and a fake tag <script>alert('x')</script> must be shown as plain text, never executed. Also: naïve, café, Ünïcödé, नमस्ते, ≈, √d, α/β.

diagram.caption: one forward pass: parallel over all tokens, repeated N times in the stack

key_takeaways: Transformers replace recurrence with attention so all positions are processed in parallel.
The same block is repeated N times; depth gives richer representations.
Everything starts with tokens → vectors and ends with a softmax over the vocabulary.

recall.q: Why can a Transformer train much faster than an RNN?
recall.a: It has no step-by-step recurrence: attention connects all positions in one matrix multiplication, so a GPU processes the whole sequence in parallel.

sections.title: tokens & embeddings
sections.subtitle: turning text into numbers

blocks.text: A chunk of text — a word, part of a word or a single character — that the model treats as one unit. Vocabularies hold 30k–200k tokens.
A learned vector (for example 768 numbers) that represents one token; similar meanings end up close together in this space.
Most LLMs use **subword tokenization** (BPE or WordPiece): frequent words stay whole, rare words split into pieces, so there are no truly unknown words.

blocks.title: the embedding lookup
blocks.text: The embedding layer is just a table of shape (vocab, d_model). Token id 412 selects row 412 — a vector the network can adjust during training.

blocks.code:
ids = tokenizer.encode("unbelievable")   # [412, 9034, 87]
vecs = embedding_table[ids]               # shape (3, 768)
print(vecs.shape)

diagram.title: from text to vectors
diagram.caption: four ideas hang off one pipeline

key_takeaways: Tokens are subword pieces, not always whole words.
An embedding is a learned row in a (vocab × d_model) table.

recall.a: A learned vector for a token; the embedding layer is a lookup table whose rows are tuned during training so related tokens sit close together.

sections.title: self-attention, step by step
sections.subtitle: queries, keys, values

blocks.text: Each token vector x is projected three ways with learned matrices: a **query** (what am I looking for?), a **key** (what do I contain?) and a **value** (what do I hand over if chosen?).

items: Compute Q = xW_Q, K = xW_K, V = xW_V for every token.
Score every pair: dot-product of a query with every key (Q·Kᵀ).
Scale by √d_k so the scores do not blow up the softmax.
Softmax each row to get attention weights that sum to 1.
Output = weights × V: a weighted average of the value vectors.

blocks.text: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q·Kᵀ / √d_k ) · V
Think of the weights as a heat-map: row i shows how much token i listens to each other token. In “the animal didn't cross because it was tired” the row for “it” is bright at “animal”.
Without the √d_k scaling the dot products grow with dimension; softmax saturates and gradients vanish — a classic exam question.

diagram.title: inside one attention head
diagram.caption: Q, K and V come from the same input — hence “self”-attention

key_takeaways: Q·Kᵀ is a similarity score between every pair of tokens.
Softmax turns scores into weights; the output is a weighted sum of values.
Cost grows with n² for sequence length n.

recall.q: Walk me through self-attention in one breath.
recall.a: Project tokens to Q, K, V; score Q against all K, scale, softmax into weights; return the weights-weighted sum of V for each token.

sections.title: multi-head attention
sections.subtitle: several views at once

blocks.text: One attention pattern cannot capture everything, so the model runs **h heads** in parallel, each with smaller Q/K/V (d_k = d_model / h). Their outputs are concatenated and mixed by one more linear layer.

items: Different heads often specialise: syntax, coreference, nearby words, rare delimiters.
Cost stays about the same as one big head because each head is smaller.
Heads are not hand-designed — they emerge during training.

diagram.title: what each head might focus on
diagram.caption: illustrative — real heads are less tidy

key_takeaways: Heads attend to different relationships in parallel.
Outputs are concatenated, then projected with W_O.

recall.a: Each head learns its own attention pattern in a smaller subspace, so the layer can track several relationships between the same tokens at once.

sections.title: positional encoding
sections.subtitle: order is not free

blocks.text: Attention treats its input as a **set**: shuffle the tokens and the scores stay the same. To restore order we add a position vector to each embedding.
PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d))   ·   PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^(2i/d))

items: Sinusoidal (original): fixed, can extrapolate to longer sequences in theory.
Learned absolute positions: a trainable table, simple, limited to the trained length.
Rotary (RoPE) and ALiBi: relative positions used by most modern LLMs.

blocks.title: why sines?
blocks.text: Each dimension is a wave of a different wavelength, like the digits of a clock; the offset between two positions becomes a simple linear function of their encodings.

diagram.title: how a token reaches attention
diagram.caption: order is injected before any attention happens

key_takeaways: Without position information “dog bites man” = “man bites dog”.
Modern models prefer relative schemes such as RoPE.

recall.q: Why does a Transformer need positional encodings?
recall.a: Attention is permutation-invariant; adding position vectors injects the order of the tokens.

sections.title: the Transformer block
sections.subtitle: attention, then think

blocks.text: A block is the repeating unit. Residual connections (“skip” paths) and layer normalisation keep very deep stacks trainable. After attention, a position-wise feed-forward network (FFN) transforms each token independently.
Adds the block's input back to its output: y = x + F(x). Gradients can flow straight through the addition.
Normalises each token vector to zero mean and unit variance, then rescales with learned parameters.
Original paper: post-norm (normalise after the add). Most modern models use pre-norm, which is more stable at scale.
The FFN is usually 4× wider than d_model and holds most of the parameters.

key_takeaways: Residual + norm make deep stacks stable.
FFN does per-token processing; attention does cross-token mixing.

recall.q: What are the two sub-layers of a block?
recall.a: Multi-head self-attention (mix across tokens) and a position-wise feed-forward network (process each token), each wrapped in residual + layer norm.

sections.title: training & the loss loop
sections.subtitle: predict, compare, nudge

blocks.text: Language models are trained with a very simple objective: **predict the next token**. The text is its own label — no human annotation is required — which is why this scales to trillions of tokens. The model sees a window of tokens, outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary and is scored with cross-entropy against the token that actually came next.

A causal mask hides future positions inside attention so token i can only attend to tokens ≤ i. During training all positions are predicted at once (teacher forcing), which is exactly where the Transformer's parallelism pays off. At inference the model must generate one token at a time, feeding each prediction back in, and a key-value cache avoids recomputing old keys and values.

items: Optimiser: Adam / AdamW with a learning-rate warm-up followed by decay.
Regularisation: dropout, weight decay, label smoothing in the original paper.
Mixed precision (fp16 / bf16) halves memory and speeds up matrix multiplications.
Gradient clipping (norm 1.0) protects against loss spikes.
Batches are huge — often millions of tokens — spread across many GPUs with data / tensor / pipeline parallelism.
Learning-rate schedule: linear warm-up for the first ~1–2% of steps, then cosine decay.
Checkpointing: save weights + optimiser state often; long runs will crash eventually.
Evaluation: track validation loss and perplexity; plot loss curves per token position.
Data matters at least as much as architecture: deduplicate, filter, balance domains.
Context length is a budget: attention memory grows with n², so long contexts need tricks such as FlashAttention.

blocks.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class TinyAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model=64, n_heads=4):
        super().__init__()
        self.h = n_heads
        self.dk = d_model // n_heads
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model)
        self.out = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)

    def forward(self, x, mask=None):
        B, T, D = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).chunk(3, dim=-1)
        # split into heads: (B, h, T, dk)
        q, k, v = [t.view(B, T, self.h, self.dk).transpose(1, 2) for t in (q, k, v)]
        scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / self.dk ** 0.5   # QK^T / sqrt(dk)
        if mask is not None:
            scores = scores.masked_fill(mask == 0, float("-inf"))
        attn = scores.softmax(dim=-1)                       # rows sum to 1
        y = (attn @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, D)
        return self.out(y)

# one training step, in 6 lines
logits = model(tokens[:, :-1])                  # predict the next token
loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(logits.flatten(0, 1), tokens[:, 1:].flatten())
loss.backward()                                 # gradients through every layer
torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
optimizer.step(); scheduler.step()              # warm-up, then decay
optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)

items: Tokenise a batch and shift it by one position to make inputs and targets.
Run the forward pass with the causal mask.
Compute cross-entropy between logits and the shifted targets.
Back-propagate; clip the gradient norm.
Optimizer step, scheduler step, zero the gradients — then repeat for the next batch.

blocks.title: perplexity in plain words
blocks.text: If a model has perplexity 20 it is, on average, as unsure as if it were choosing uniformly among 20 equally likely next tokens. Lower is better.
When a loss curve suddenly spikes, check the data shard, the learning rate and the gradient norm — in that order.

Fine-tuning adapts a pre-trained model to a task using far less data. Parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA freeze the original weights and train small low-rank update matrices, which cuts memory dramatically and makes it possible to keep many task adapters side by side.

key_takeaways: The training signal is simply “predict the next token”.
Causal masking + teacher forcing = parallel training, sequential generation.
Optimiser tricks (warm-up, clipping, mixed precision) make large runs stable.
Fine-tuning and LoRA reuse pre-trained weights cheaply.

recall.q: Why is generation slower than training per token?
recall.a: Training predicts all positions in one parallel pass; generation must emit tokens one by one, each depending on the previous, even with a KV cache.

sections.title: a short history

blocks.text: The ideas arrived in steps: attention first helped RNN translators, then replaced them, then became the backbone of general-purpose language models.

items: 2014: Bahdanau attention lets a translator look back at the source sentence.
2017: the Transformer — attention only, parallel training.
2018: BERT (encoder) and GPT (decoder) show pre-train-then-fine-tune works.
2020: GPT-3 shows in-context learning at 175B parameters.
2022: instruction tuning + RLHF turn LLMs into assistants.

diagram.title: milestones
diagram.caption: each step kept the attention core and changed scale or training

key_takeaways: Scale + data + the same attention core drove the progress.
Instruction tuning made models usable by non-experts.

recall.q: What changed between GPT-2 and GPT-3?
recall.a: Mainly scale: far more parameters and data, which unlocked in-context (few-shot) learning without any weight updates.

sections.title: model families & scaling
sections.subtitle: encoder, decoder or both

blocks.text: The original Transformer had an encoder and a decoder. Later models keep one half depending on the job.

items: Encoder-only (BERT): bidirectional, great for classification and embeddings.
Decoder-only (GPT, LLaMA): causal, the standard for text generation.
Encoder-decoder (T5): reads input fully, then generates output — translation, summarisation.

blocks.text: Scaling laws: loss falls smoothly as a power law in parameters, data and compute — which is why bigger runs were funded.

diagram.title: the family tree
diagram.caption: all share the same attention block

key_takeaways: Pick the half of the Transformer that matches the task.
Scaling laws predict gains from more parameters, data and compute.

recall.q: Why are most chat models decoder-only?
recall.a: Next-token prediction with a causal mask is simple, scales well and handles any text-in/text-out task in a single architecture.

glossary.definition: A unit of text (word piece) the model reads.
A learned vector representing a token.
The three projections of a token used by attention: what it seeks, what it offers, what it passes on.
Turns arbitrary scores into positive weights that sum to 1.
Several attention heads in parallel, each in a smaller subspace.
Extra vector that tells the model where a token sits in the sequence.
Adds a layer's input to its output: y = x + F(x).
Normalises each token vector across its features.
Blocks attention to future tokens so generation stays left-to-right.
Feeding the true previous tokens during training so all positions are learned in parallel.
Stored keys and values of earlier tokens, reused during generation.
exp(cross-entropy): the effective number of equally likely choices.
Fine-tuning with small trainable low-rank updates on frozen weights.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback to align outputs.
Power-law relation between loss and model size, data, compute.
Byte-pair encoding: merges frequent character pairs to build a subword vocabulary.

recap.title: the whole picture, recapped
points: Each block: multi-head self-attention mixes tokens, the FFN refines each token; residual + norm keep it trainable.
Attention = softmax(Q·Kᵀ/√d)·V, run in several heads.
Training predicts the next token; a causal mask makes it parallel.
Variants: encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder-decoder; scale drives quality.
